newsitem.title: USA: Ford to put slower airbags in all '98 models.
newsitem.headline: Ford to put slower airbags in all '98 models.

text.p: Ford Motor Co., jumping ahead of other automakers, said Thursday it will install slower inflating airbags in all of its 1998 model year cars and light trucks.
The announcement comes a month after federal regulators revised air bag safety test rules, clearing the way for automakers to lower the 200 mph deploying force by as much as 35 percent.
Air bags were originally designed to protect an unbelted 167-pound male. They are credited with saving about 1,750 lives since being introduced in the 1980s.
But air bag deployments have also been blamed for more than 60 deaths, including 38 children, prompting safety advocates to demand changes.

Ford, which has cultivated a strong safety image, said its first vehicle with a so-called depowered air bag will be the 1998 Lincoln Navigator, a luxury version of the Ford Expedition full-size sport utility vehicle that goes on sale July 1.

After that, every Ford and Lincoln Mercury vehicle line in North America will have what Ford calls Second Generation air bags. The new system will be identifiable by a Second Generation window designation visible on both driver and passenger sides.
Anticipating the rules change, Ford late last year started testing the new air bags in all of its models to tailor an optimum inflation rate for smaller females and "out-of-position" children.

The company has now come up with reductions of 25 percent to 35 percent, depending on the vehicle, said spokesman Dave Giroux. He declined to specify the cost to Ford, but said it would not add to vehicle prices.

Chrysler, the U.S. No. 3 automaker, also said Thursday all of its 1998 model vehicles will have air bags that have been depowered to some degree. However, unlike Ford, Chrysler's programme will not be fully implemented until the start of the 1999 model year in the fall of 1998.
General Motors Corp., which has the most models of the Big Three, said between one-third and one-half of its 1998 model vehicles will have depowered air bags.

Toyota Motor Corp., the largest Japanese automaker, plans to begin phasing in depowered air bags this fall with 1998 model vehicles, said spokesman Jeremy Barnes. All Toyota vehicles in the United States will have the new air bags by the fall of 1999.
Ford will receive its depowered air bag modules from Morton International Inc. and TRW Inc.. The deployment force is lessened by reducing the amount of propellant in the air bag module.

"Our goal was to offer these new and improved air bags to all of our customers as quickly and completely as possible, certainly by the 1998 model year, and that's what we have done," Helen Petrauskas, Ford vice president for Environmental and Safety Engineering, said in a statement.
